title: Massachusetts Schedule VI
learning_objectives: Recognize Schedule VI as the Massachusetts controlled-substance schedule for prescription drugs outside Schedules I through V, rather than as a federal controlled schedule.
Apply Massachusetts prescription elements, oral documentation, electronic-prescribing exceptions, and transfer rules without inventing federal consequences.
Apply the Schedule VI validity clock and the additional-drug consequences instead of treating Schedule VI as a consequence-free label.
Recognise that the Schedule VI classification carries its own scope-of-practice consequence for who may transfer a prescription.
Identify every date gate that can bar a Schedule VI prescription, including the out-of-state 30-day window that sits alongside the one-year validity clock.

orientation.text: Massachusetts Schedule VI is the residual schedule: it holds prescription drugs that Massachusetts has not otherwise placed in Schedules I through V. It is a controlled-substance schedule all the same. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 defines a controlled substance as a drug, substance, controlled substance analogue or immediate precursor in any schedule or class referred to in that chapter, and s. 2(a) establishes the sixth schedule alongside the five that incorporate the federal schedules, so the ordinary prescription drug that carries no federal schedule is, in Massachusetts, a Schedule VI controlled substance. Two consequences follow, and they pull in opposite directions. Schedule VI has no federal counterpart -- 105 CMR 700.002(A) through (E) define Massachusetts Schedules I through V as the drugs listed in 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15, and 700.002(F) leaves Schedule VI the prescription drugs outside them -- so Schedule VI status does not by itself make a drug federally controlled, and federal controlled-substance mechanics do not automatically travel with the label. Because Schedule VI is nonetheless a Massachusetts controlled-substance schedule, a Massachusetts rule that speaks to controlled substances reaches Schedule VI unless that rule carves Schedule VI out: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(f), for instance, allows no refill of a controlled-substance prescription unless the original provides for refilling and specifies the number of refills. Reading the label as a synonym for unregulated is the single most productive source of wrong answers in this area.

Every rule taught in this section is Massachusetts law, and it does not all come from one regulator. M.G.L. c. 94C is the statute above both. The Department of Public Health writes 105 CMR 700.000 and 105 CMR 721.000, and from there come the classification itself, the prescription-format scheme, the electronic-prescribing exceptions and the prescription monitoring program. The Board of Registration in Pharmacy writes 247 CMR, and from there come the Schedule VI validity clock, the within-date counting convention and the transfer framework. Some duties are stated twice over. A customer identifier must be presented under the Board's 247 CMR 9.04(14) and, for a pharmacy subject to the monitoring-program reporting requirement, under the Department's 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3); M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c)(2) directs the Department to require each pharmacy to collect and report a customer identification number for each monitored prescription. Even inside the Board's own chapter a Schedule VI question can turn on two different one-year rules that sit in two different sections of 247 CMR 9.00 and answer two different questions: 247 CMR 9.04(12) says how long the prescription stays valid, and 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) says how long it stays transferable. Neither restates the other, and a candidate who has collapsed them into one rule will misread whichever question is actually being asked.

On format, Massachusetts starts from a default that every prescription generated in the Commonwealth must be electronic, and then lists the prescriptions excepted from it. Schedule VI is one of the enumerated exceptions, at 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9), which is why a Schedule VI prescription may lawfully arrive written or oral. The exception is narrow in exactly the way candidates tend to forget: it lifts the electronic-format mandate and nothing else. A written Schedule VI prescription must still carry the practitioner's signature and be either transmitted by facsimile or similar technology or written on a tamper-resistant form, and a prescription in a non-conforming format is invalid and shall not be filled. An oral Schedule VI prescription must still be reduced to writing immediately with the information the statute requires. Among the oral-prescription duties, the one Schedule VI escapes is the practitioner's later follow-up prescription: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) says in its own terms that its requirements do not apply to controlled substances in Schedule VI, and the follow-up in 105 CMR 721.070(B) is written for oral prescriptions in Schedules II through V. The Failover device points the same way: it is defined as a document that originates as a Schedule VI electronic prescription, so no other schedule can produce one.

A Schedule VI prescription can be stopped by more than one clock, and the exam rewards knowing which clock the facts have started. The general one is the validity limit: a prescription for a Schedule VI medication is valid for one year from the date of issue, and a licensee may not refill it after one year. A second one attaches to the prescriber rather than the drug. An authorized out-of-state practitioner may issue a Schedule III through VI prescription for filling in Massachusetts, but M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) authorizes filling only prescriptions issued within the preceding thirty days, and it is that paragraph, not the one-year rule, that makes the out-of-state prescription fillable here in the first place. Both clocks are counted the same way, because in determining whether a prescription is within date the pharmacist counts the day after the prescription was written as day one. The two clocks fail differently, and the fourteen-day continuation belongs to only one of them: 247 CMR 9.04(12) opens it where a Schedule VI prescription expires or has no remaining refills and the pharmacist is unable to obtain prescriber authorization in a timely manner. Nothing in it reopens the thirty-day authorization in s. 18(c), so an out-of-state prescription past that window is not a candidate for a bridge supply on the strength of the continuation.

Transfer is the other place where the Schedule VI label changes the analysis, and it does so in the pharmacy's direction as well as the patient's. Under 247 CMR 9.14 a pharmacy shall transfer a prescription to another pharmacy at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, and it may act as the patient's agent to facilitate that transfer. A pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription, so neither a standing refusal to transfer nor a transfer charge is a matter the pharmacy gets to decide for itself. Schedule VI prescriptions transfer in the same manner as Schedule III through V prescriptions, carrying up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized, subject to the separate one-year transfer bar. Schedule VI is also the only schedule for which a certified pharmacy technician may perform the transfer, and then only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

Finally, the Schedule VI label is not a promise that no monitoring or identification duty will ever attach. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(a)(1) has the Department monitor all schedule II to V controlled substances and certain additional drugs, meaning substances the Department determines to carry a bona fide potential for abuse, and 105 CMR 700.001 defines an Additional Drug as a controlled substance in Schedule VI so determined. The Commissioner may make that determination for the purposes of 105 CMR 700.012, weighing factors such as a risk of addiction, known recreational use, known regular diversion for misuse, or a known contribution to overdose, and on making it notifies all dispensers that they must begin reporting the dispensing of that drug. Once a Schedule VI drug is an additional drug, dispensing it requires a customer identifier from the ultimate user or their agent, subject to the documented-hardship route, under both 247 CMR 9.04(14) and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3); the Failover route closes, because a Failover does not qualify where the prescription is for an additional drug; and the dispensing has to be reported on two clocks that apply together. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c) requires the information to be submitted at least once every 24 hours, and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5) requires transmission by the end of the next business day, each transmission carrying everything dispensed since the previous one. The operative deadline is whichever of the two arrives first, and across a weekend or a holiday that is always the statute: a Friday dispensing cannot wait for the end of Monday, which the regulation read alone would allow. The label describes the starting point, not the whole of the drug's regulatory position.

comparison_tables.title: Three date gates on a Schedule VI prescription, and how the days are counted
columns: What happens once it is passed

cells: Prescription validity
One year from the date of issue
A licensee may not refill the prescription. If prescriber authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner, the professional-judgment continuation becomes available on its own conditions.
Transfer of a prescription authorizing refills
One year from the date the prescription was issued
The pharmacy may not transfer it. This says nothing about whether the prescription is still fillable where it sits.
Out-of-state prescriber, Schedules III through VI
Issued within the preceding thirty days

comparison_tables.title: What the Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception removes, and what survives it

cells: Duty to issue the prescription electronically
No. Schedule VI is an enumerated ePrescribing exception, so the prescription may be issued written or oral.
Statutory prescription elements
Yes. The exception addresses format, not content.
Written-format requirements: signature, plus facsimile transmission or a tamper-resistant form
Yes, and a prescription in a non-conforming format is invalid and shall not be filled.
Immediate reduction of an oral prescription to writing with the required information
Yes. The pharmacist's documentation duty is untouched by the exception.
M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(a) and (b)
Practitioner's later follow-up prescription after an oral order
No. The subsection states that its requirements do not apply to controlled substances in Schedule VI.
Pharmacist duty to verify that the prescription properly falls within an exception
No such duty is imposed on the receiving pharmacist.

comparison_tables.title: Transfer of a Schedule VI prescription: what 247 CMR 9.14 settles for the pharmacy

cells: May the pharmacy decline the request as a matter of store policy?
No. A pharmacy shall transfer a prescription to another pharmacy at the request of a patient or the patient's agent, in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy.
May the pharmacy arrange the transfer on the patient's behalf?
Yes. The pharmacy may act as the patient's agent in order to facilitate a transfer.
May the pharmacy charge for the transfer?
No. A pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription.
How many refills move with it?
Up to the maximum number of remaining refills authorized by the prescriber, Schedule VI transferring in the same manner as Schedules III through V.
Is the prescription too old to transfer?
It is once it is more than one year from the date the prescription was issued.
May a certified pharmacy technician carry it out?
Yes, for Schedule VI only, and only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient asks Pharmacy B to obtain a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription from Pharmacy A. The prescription was issued ten months ago and has three authorized refills remaining. Pharmacy A says it does not transfer prescriptions as a matter of store policy, and that if it did it would charge the patient a transfer fee first. Pharmacy B has a certified pharmacy technician available and the pharmacist on duty approves the technician's participation.
steps: Classify the drug before anything else. It is not in Massachusetts Schedules I through V, so it is a Schedule VI controlled substance under Massachusetts law, and because no federal schedule lists it the federal transfer mechanics do not reach it.

Check the age of the prescription against the transfer bar rather than the validity clock. 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) bars transfer of a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills more than one year from the date it was issued; ten months is inside that limit.

Test Pharmacy A's policy against 247 CMR 9.14(1). A pharmacy shall transfer a prescription at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, so a standing refusal to transfer cannot stand against the request.
Test the fee against 247 CMR 9.14(3), which provides that a pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription. There is no discretion to price the transfer.

Settle what moves. Schedule VI prescriptions transfer in the same manner as Schedules III through V, and may be transferred up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized, so all three remaining refills may travel.

Settle who may act. A certified pharmacy technician may perform a Schedule VI transfer with the approval of the pharmacist on duty, and that authority is confined to Schedule VI; do not generalise it to any other schedule.
worked_examples.resolution: The transfer proceeds promptly, without a fee, carrying the three remaining refills, and the certified technician may carry it out with the pharmacist's approval. The error the scenario invites is treating a no-transfer policy and a transfer charge as pharmacy discretion, when 247 CMR 9.14(1) and 9.14(3) remove both; a second error is reaching for a six-month cutoff in place of the one-year transfer limit.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient presents a Schedule VI prescription written forty-five days ago by a practitioner licensed and registered in New Hampshire, whose address on the prescription is a New Hampshire office. The patient points out that Massachusetts Schedule VI prescriptions are good for a year, so the prescription must still be fillable.
steps: Confirm the patient is right about the clock they have named. Under 247 CMR 9.04(12) the prescription is valid for one year from the date of issue, and forty-five days is well inside that.

Then ask the question the patient has not asked: what makes an out-of-state practitioner's prescription fillable in Massachusetts at all. That authorization is M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c), which reaches prescriptions in Schedules III to VI inclusive.

Read the limit that paragraph attaches to its own grant. It is valid only for the purpose of authorizing the filling of prescriptions issued within the preceding thirty days, so it is a second date gate rather than a restatement of the first.
Count the days the way the Board directs, taking the day after the prescription was written as day one. Forty-five days still falls outside the thirty-day window however the count is started.

Do not look for a verification step that will rescue it. The express duty to verify the prescription by telephone or other means runs to Schedules III through V; for a Schedule VI prescription the pharmacist's duty is the general one to determine that the prescription is authentic and valid, and neither duty extends the thirty-day window.

Do not reach for the fourteen-day continuation either. 247 CMR 9.04(12) opens it where a Schedule VI prescription expires or has no remaining refills and authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner; this prescription has not expired, and in any event nothing in the continuation reopens the thirty-day authorization in s. 18(c).
worked_examples.resolution: The prescription may not be filled on the out-of-state authorization, because the paragraph that authorizes filling it here reaches only prescriptions issued within the preceding thirty days. The error the scenario invites is answering from the one-year Schedule VI validity clock alone and never asking where the prescriber wrote from.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient arrives on a Saturday evening out of a maintenance medication. The Schedule VI prescription on file was issued fourteen months ago and shows refills that were never used. A colleague says the prescription has plainly expired, so the fourteen-day continuation is simply what you dispense in that situation.
steps: Establish that the prescription itself is spent. It was valid for one year from the date of issue, and a licensee may not refill a Schedule VI prescription after one year, so unused refills on a fourteen-month-old prescription do not survive the expiry.

Read the continuation as the conditional allowance it is. It opens where a Schedule VI prescription expires or has no remaining refills AND the pharmacist is unable to obtain prescriber authorization in a timely manner; the inability condition governs the expiry branch exactly as it governs the no-refills-remaining branch.

Attempt the authorization first. Try the prescriber, or whoever is covering, and record the attempt. Only once authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner does the professional-judgment allowance become available at all.

If it does open, respect the ceiling. The pharmacist in his or her professional judgment may dispense a quantity not to exceed fourteen days or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging. It is a bridge, not a refill, and it does not renew the expired prescription.

Check the setting before applying any of this. 247 CMR 9.04(15) excludes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 247 CMR 9.04(12), so the validity clock and the continuation attached to it do not reach that facility type.
worked_examples.resolution: Attempt the prescriber before dispensing anything; the fourteen-day continuation becomes available only after that attempt fails to produce timely authorization. The error the colleague makes is reading the expiry branch as self-executing, which drops the inability-to-obtain-authorization condition the regulation attaches to both branches.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Massachusetts Schedule VI carries two separate one-year rules. State each one and what it measures.
retrieval_prompts.answer: 247 CMR 9.04(12): a Schedule VI prescription is valid for one year from the date of issue and may not be refilled after one year. 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c): a pharmacy may not transfer a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills more than one year from the date the prescription was issued. One measures fillability, the other transferability.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A pharmacy tells a patient it does not transfer prescriptions, and that in any event it charges for a transfer. Which two provisions dispose of that?
retrieval_prompts.answer: 247 CMR 9.14(1) requires the pharmacy to transfer at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, and 247 CMR 9.14(3) provides that a pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Besides the one-year validity clock, what second date gate can stop a Schedule VI prescription, and where does it come from?
retrieval_prompts.answer: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c): an authorized out-of-state practitioner's prescription in Schedules III to VI inclusive may be filled in Massachusetts only if it was issued within the preceding thirty days.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which oral-prescription duty does Schedule VI escape, and which does it keep?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It escapes the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) follow-up prescription, which states that its requirements do not apply to Schedule VI. It keeps the duty to reduce the oral prescription to writing immediately with the information the statute requires.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: The Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception sits at 105 CMR 721.070(A)(9). What does it not excuse?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It lifts the electronic-format mandate only. The statutory prescription elements still apply, a written prescription must still carry the practitioner's signature and be transmitted by facsimile or written on a tamper-resistant form, and a prescription in a non-conforming format is invalid and shall not be filled.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What turns an ordinary Schedule VI drug into one carrying monitoring and identification duties?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The Commissioner's determination under 105 CMR 700.012(C)(8) that it is an additional drug carrying a bona fide potential for abuse. On that determination dispensers are notified that they must begin reporting it, and a customer identifier is required at dispensing under 247 CMR 9.04(14) and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3), subject to the documented-hardship route. The reporting then runs on two clocks: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c) requires submission at least once every 24 hours, and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5) requires transmission by the end of the next business day, covering everything dispensed since the previous transmission.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A document that began as a Schedule VI electronic prescription failed in transmission and arrived as a computer-generated facsimile. What is it, and what does it not owe?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A Failover. It is considered an oral prescription and requires no written or electronic follow-up prescription, provided the three conditions in 105 CMR 721.020(G) hold and the prescription is not for an additional drug.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: In deciding whether a prescription is within date, which day is day one?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The day after the prescription was written; the issue date itself is not counted.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name two things 105 CMR 721.020 requires on the face of a prescription that the element list in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(a) does not.
retrieval_prompts.answer: The quantity of dosage units, under 105 CMR 721.020(D)(3), alongside the name, dosage and strength per dosage unit that the statute requires; and the name of the supervising qualified healthcare professional on a prescription issued by a certified nurse practitioner, psychiatric nurse mental health clinical specialist or certified registered nurse anesthetist who is not authorized for independent practice, under 721.020(E). The refill statement in 721.020(D)(6) is not one of the additions, because s. 22(a) requires it too.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A Schedule VI additional drug is dispensed on a Friday afternoon. When must the dispensing reach the Department?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Whichever limit arrives first, because both apply: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c) requires the information to be submitted at least once every 24 hours, and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5) requires transmission by the end of the next business day, carrying everything dispensed since the previous transmission. Across the weekend the statute is the stricter, so waiting for the end of Monday is not an option.

quick_review.text: Massachusetts Schedule VI includes prescription drugs not otherwise placed in Massachusetts Schedules I through V.

Every Schedule VI drug is a controlled substance under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 and s. 2(a), while 105 CMR 700.002(A) through (E) make Massachusetts Schedules I through V the federal lists, so Schedule VI is a Massachusetts controlled-substance schedule with no federal counterpart; a Massachusetts rule written for controlled substances, such as the refill condition in s. 23(f), reaches it unless the rule carves Schedule VI out.
Schedule VI prescriptions are excepted from the Massachusetts electronic-prescribing requirement, while all other validity requirements remain applicable.
An oral controlled-substance prescription must be reduced to writing immediately with the required information; the separate duty to deliver a later follow-up prescription does not reach Schedule VI.
A Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription is valid for one year from the date of issue, and a licensee may not refill it after one year.

A Schedule VI drug the Department designates as an additional drug becomes reportable to the prescription monitoring program by a pharmacy subject to 105 CMR 700.012, and its dispensing requires a customer identifier, subject to the documented-hardship route.

A pharmacy shall transfer a prescription to another pharmacy at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, and may act as the patient's agent to facilitate the transfer; a standing policy of refusing transfers cannot displace that duty.
A pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription.
Schedule VI is the only schedule for which a certified pharmacy technician may perform a prescription transfer, and then only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

A Schedule VI prescription may be transferred up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized under 247 CMR 9.14(4)(b); the federal one-time transfer limit in 21 CFR 1306.25(a) reaches prescriptions for substances listed in federal Schedules III, IV and V, so it does not reach a Schedule VI drug that no federal schedule lists.

A prescription written by an authorized out-of-state practitioner is fillable in Massachusetts under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c), which reaches Schedules III to VI inclusive and authorizes filling only prescriptions issued within the preceding thirty days; that is a second date gate on a Schedule VI prescription, distinct from the one-year validity clock.

Prescription monitoring data for a reportable dispensing runs on two limits that apply together: at least once every 24 hours under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c), and by the end of the next business day under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5), each transmission covering everything dispensed since the previous one.

decision_logic.condition: A prescription drug is not in Massachusetts Schedules I-V.
decision_logic.action: Classify it under Schedule VI, then identify the separate rule governing validity, documentation, dispensing, or transfer.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule VI prescription is written or oral rather than electronic.
decision_logic.action: Do not reject it solely for that format; apply the Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception and all remaining prescription requirements, including the form requirements that still govern a written prescription.

decision_logic.condition: A patient requests transfer of a Schedule VI prescription with authorized refills remaining.
decision_logic.action: Act on the request rather than declining it: 247 CMR 9.14(1) requires the pharmacy to transfer at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, 9.14(2) lets the pharmacy act as the patient's agent to facilitate it, and 9.14(3) forbids charging a fee for the transfer. Then apply the Schedule VI mechanics under 247 CMR 9.14(4): the prescription transfers in the same manner as a Schedule III through V prescription and may carry up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized, that regulation bars the transfer more than one year after issue, and a certified pharmacy technician may carry it out with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule VI prescription has expired, being presented more than one year after its issue date, or has no refills remaining, and in either case the pharmacist is unable to obtain prescriber authorization in a timely manner.
decision_logic.action: Do not refill it. The inability to obtain timely prescriber authorization conditions both branches equally, so attempt the prescriber first in the expired case exactly as in the no-refills-remaining case. Only once that attempt has failed may the pharmacist, in professional judgment, dispense a quantity not to exceed 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging.

decision_logic.condition: The Schedule VI medication being dispensed has been designated an additional drug by the Department.
decision_logic.action: Obtain a customer identifier under 247 CMR 9.04(14) and 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3), using the documented hardship route only on its own terms, and treat the dispensing as reportable, submitting at least once every 24 hours under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c) and by the end of the next business day under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5).

decision_logic.condition: The Schedule VI prescription was written by a practitioner licensed and registered outside Massachusetts.
decision_logic.action: Apply the out-of-state date gate before the validity clock: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) authorizes filling such a prescription only if it was issued within the preceding thirty days, counting the day after it was written as day one. Determine that the prescription is authentic and valid; note that the express telephone-or-other-means verification requirement runs to Schedules III through V rather than to Schedule VI.

ma_vs_federal.text: Schedule VI is a Massachusetts controlled-substance classification: it makes the drug a controlled substance under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 and s. 2(a), and it does not itself make the drug federally controlled, because Massachusetts Schedules I through V are the federal lists that Schedule VI sits outside.
A Schedule VI drug the Department designates as an additional drug carries Massachusetts prescription-monitoring and customer-identifier duties that the Schedule VI label alone does not imply.

The Massachusetts route for an out-of-state practitioner's prescription is M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c), which reaches Schedules III to VI inclusive; because Schedule VI has no federal counterpart, that thirty-day window is a purely Massachusetts limit and has no federal analogue to be read against it.

exceptions.text: The Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception removes that format mandate, not the required prescription elements or oral documentation duties.

Where a Schedule VI prescription has expired or has no remaining refills and prescriber authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner, the pharmacist may in professional judgment dispense a quantity not exceeding 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use packaging.

247 CMR 9.04(15) excludes institutional sterile compounding pharmacies from 247 CMR 9.04(12), and from 9.04(10) and 9.04(14) as well, so the Board's Schedule VI validity clock, its day-counting convention and its customer-identifier requirement do not reach that facility type. The exclusion reaches only those Board paragraphs: for a pharmacy subject to 105 CMR 700.012, the Department's own customer-identifier requirement in 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3) continues to apply.
In deciding whether a prescription is within date the pharmacist counts the day after it was written as day one, so the Schedule VI one-year period does not include the issue date itself.

The follow-up duty Schedule VI escapes is the practitioner's obligation under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 20(c) to deliver an electronic prescription within 2 days, or a written one within not more than 7 days, or the shorter period federal law requires, where the prescriber holds an electronic-prescribing exception under s. 23(h); the parallel follow-up in 105 CMR 721.070(B) is written for oral prescriptions in Schedules II through V and does not reach Schedule VI either.

The Failover is a Schedule VI device: a document that began as a Schedule VI electronic prescription, failed in transmission and arrived as a computer-generated facsimile counts as an oral prescription needing no follow-up, provided its three conditions hold and the drug is not an additional drug.

105 CMR 700.012 does not apply to dispensing pursuant to a medication order to an inpatient in a hospital, so neither the monitoring-program reporting duty nor the Department's customer-identifier requirement reaches that dispensing, whatever the drug; 105 CMR 700.012(A)(1) otherwise reaches every pharmacy registered with the Commissioner that dispenses a Schedule II through V controlled substance or an additional drug pursuant to a prescription.

timing_deadlines.event: Remaining-refill transfer of a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills
timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not more than 1 year after issue
timing_deadlines.consequence: 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) does not permit that remaining-refill transfer after the regulatory one-year limit.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: 1 year from the date of issue
timing_deadlines.consequence: A licensee may not refill a Schedule VI prescription after one year.

timing_deadlines.event: Filling in Massachusetts a Schedule III through VI prescription issued by an authorized out-of-state practitioner
timing_deadlines.consequence: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) authorizes filling only prescriptions issued within that window, so an older out-of-state Schedule VI prescription is barred even though the one-year validity period has not run.

timing_deadlines.event: Transmission of prescription monitoring data for a reportable dispensing, under the Department's regulation
timing_deadlines.timeframe: By the end of the next business day
timing_deadlines.consequence: 105 CMR 700.012(A)(5) also requires each transmission to carry every controlled substance dispensed since the previous one.

timing_deadlines.event: Submission of prescription monitoring information, under the statute
timing_deadlines.consequence: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c) sets this limit alongside the Department's transmission requirement, so a dispensing reported only at the end of the next business day is late whenever more than 24 hours have passed since the pharmacy's previous submission, as after a Friday dispensing held until Monday.

forms_records.text: The pharmacist must immediately reduce an oral controlled-substance prescription to writing with the required Massachusetts prescription information.

A customer identifier must be obtained when dispensing a Schedule VI additional drug, under 247 CMR 9.04(14) and, for a pharmacy subject to 105 CMR 700.012, under 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3); the hardship route requires a documented reason and the recipient's printed name and address and signature, with an electronic signature in the case of an electronic prescription.

A written Schedule VI prescription must carry the practitioner's signature and must either be transmitted by facsimile or similar technology or be written on a tamper-resistant form consistent with federal Medicaid requirements; a prescription in a non-conforming format is invalid and may not be filled.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(a) requires a practitioner who dispenses a controlled substance by issuing a written or electronic prescription to state on it the practitioner's name, address and registration number, the date of delivery of the prescription, the name, dosage and strength per dosage unit of the controlled substance, the name and address of the patient unless it is a veterinary prescription, the directions for use and any cautionary statements required, and a statement indicating the number of times to be refilled. Read that as the list the statute itself imposes, not as a closed inventory of everything a Massachusetts prescription must carry: the Massachusetts prescription-format regulations reach the same prescription and impose their own requirements alongside the statute.

The format regulation states content the statutory element list does not, and relaxes the patient-identification element in cases the statute does not name: 105 CMR 721.020(D)(3) requires the QUANTITY OF DOSAGE UNITS alongside the name, dosage and strength per dosage unit; (D)(6) repeats the statutory statement indicating the number of times to be refilled; and under (D)(4) the patient's name and address MAY BE LEFT BLANK not only on a veterinary prescription but also on one for naloxone or another Department-approved opioid antagonist and on one issued under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7), for expedited partner therapy for the treatment of chlamydia, or (A)(12), for a declared public health emergency, for diseases dangerous to public health including sexually transmitted infections, or for any other urgent public health matter.

A prescription issued by a certified nurse practitioner, psychiatric nurse mental health clinical specialist or certified registered nurse anesthetist must also carry the name of the supervising qualified healthcare professional, unless that nurse is authorized for independent practice.

role_duties.duty: Validate required prescription elements even when the Schedule VI electronic-prescribing exception applies.
Check the Schedule VI validity clock and any additional-drug designation before dispensing rather than treating Schedule VI as consequence-free.
Act on a patient's or agent's transfer request in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy, and transfer without charging a fee.
Perform a prescription transfer only for Schedule VI, and only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

common_traps.text: Reading the electronic-prescribing exception as an exemption from all prescription validity requirements is incorrect.
Treating Schedule VI as a federal schedule creates legal consequences that the Massachusetts classification does not supply.

The one-year rule in 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) governs transfer of a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills and is separate from the one-year prescription validity limit in 247 CMR 9.04(12); neither should be restated as the other.
Concluding that Schedule VI never triggers identification or monitoring-program duties overlooks Schedule VI drugs designated as additional drugs.
Generalising the certified-technician transfer authority beyond Schedule VI ignores the word only in the regulation.
Reading the electronic-prescribing exception as removing every format requirement leaves the pharmacist filling a written prescription that no permitted format supports.

Treating a refusal to transfer, or a charge for transferring, as a matter of pharmacy discretion overlooks the affirmative timely-transfer duty in 247 CMR 9.14(1) and the fee prohibition in 247 CMR 9.14(3).

Treating the one-year validity clock as the only date gate on a Schedule VI prescription misses the separate thirty-day limit M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(c) places on an out-of-state practitioner's Schedule III through VI prescription.

Reciting the M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(a) elements as the complete set of content and exception rules for a Massachusetts prescription treats a statutory list as exhaustive, when the prescription-format regulations govern the same prescription in their own right.

Naming the veterinary prescription as the only case where the patient's name and address may be left blank misses the naloxone and opioid-antagonist limb and the two ePrescribing-exception limbs in 105 CMR 721.020(D)(4).

Reading Schedule VI as a label outside controlled-substance law misses M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 1 and s. 2(a), which make a Schedule VI drug a Massachusetts controlled substance, and with it every Massachusetts controlled-substance rule that does not carve Schedule VI out.

Teaching the monitoring deadline as the end of the next business day alone drops the statutory limit in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 24A(c), which requires submission at least once every 24 hours and is the stricter of the two across a weekend or holiday.

Reading the 247 CMR 9.04(15) exclusion as ending the customer-identifier duty for an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy overlooks the Department's separate requirement in 105 CMR 700.012(A)(3).
